### Description

In `lib/response.js`, the documentation comment for `res.sendFile()` still uses the following example on line 367:

```js
res.send(403, 'Sorry! you can\'t see that.');
```

This uses the old `res.send(status, body)` syntax, which was deprecated in Express 4.7.0 and removed in Express 5 according to the documentations.
The official Express 5 API documentation already uses the updated syntax, but the example in `lib/response.js` hasn't been updated.

References:
1. Source code: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/master/lib/response.js#L367
2. Express 4 API documentation: https://expressjs.com/en/4x/api/response/
3. Express 5 release announcement: https://expressjs.com/en/blog/2024-10-15-v5-release/
4. Express 5 API documentation: https://expressjs.com/en/5x/api/response/

### Expectations

Update the example in `lib/response.js` to use the supported Express 5 syntax:

```js
res.status(403).send('Sorry! you can\'t see that.');
```
This would make the example consistent with the official Express 5 API documentation.
I'm happy to submit a pull request to update this example if you'd like.
items.title: Outdated res.send() syntax in lib/response.js documentation example

Related to #7562, but for Express 4.x.

The Express 4.x branch currently specifies "body-parser": "~1.20.5". Could this be updated to "body-parser": "~1.20.9"?

[GHSA-27r3-jxmh-p828](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-27r3-jxmh-p828) affects body-parser 1.x versions below 1.20.9. A crafted compressed request can cause an uncaught exception and terminate the application.

## Environment information

**Version**: 5.3.0 (also current `master`)

**Platform**: Windows 11 x64 (not platform specific)

**Node.js version**: 22.23.4

**Any other relevant information**: Happens with any view engine. Express 4 was affected only with asynchronous engines (see #4060).

## What steps will reproduce the bug?

```js
const express = require('express')
const fs = require('node:fs')
const path = require('node:path')

const app = express()
// any engine; a minimal one that returns the file contents
app.engine('html', (file, options, callback) => fs.readFile(file, 'utf8', callback))
app.set('views', path.join(__dirname, 'views')) // contains index.html
app.set('view engine', 'html')

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.end('already sent')
  res.render('index') // a bug in app code, e.g. rendering after another response was sent
})

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  console.log('error handler:', err.code) // never reached
  next(err)
})

app.listen(3000)
```

Request `GET /`.

## What is the expected behavior?

The `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` error thrown by `res.send()` in the default `res.render()` callback is passed to `next(err)` and reaches the error handlers, like other errors in a route.

## What do you see instead?

The process crashes with an uncaught exception (exit code 1):

```
node:_http_outgoing:700
    throw new ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT('set');
    ^

Error [ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT]: Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client
    at ServerResponse.setHeader (node:_http_outgoing:700:11)
    at ServerResponse.header (node_modules/express/lib/response.js:685:10)
    at ServerResponse.contentType (node_modules/express/lib/response.js:513:15)
    at ServerResponse.send (node_modules/express/lib/response.js:143:14)
    at done (node_modules/express/lib/response.js:916:10)
    at onRender (node_modules/express/lib/view.js:141:23)
    at FSReqCallback.readFileAfterClose [as oncomplete] (node:internal/fs/read/context:68:3) {
  code: 'ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT'
}
```

The default callback calls `res.send()` from the view engine callback. Since 5.0, `View.prototype.render` always invokes that callback asynchronously (`process.nextTick`), so the `try`/`catch` in `tryRender` no longer covers it, and any throw from `res.send()` there escapes.

## Additional information

I opened #7559 with a fix and a test: errors thrown by `res.send()` in the default callback are forwarded to `next()`.

Hi! 🙂 `res.send()` with a typed array that is not a `Uint8Array`, for example a `Uint16Array`, gives two different results. The result depends on the `etag` setting and on the length of the array.

## Environment information

**Version**: express 5.3.0

**Platform**: Darwin 27.0.0

**Node.js version**: v24.21.0

**Any other relevant information**: None.

## What steps will reproduce the bug?

```js
const express = require('express')

async function run (etag, length) {
  const app = express()
  app.set('etag', etag)
  app.get('/', (req, res) => res.send(new Uint16Array(length).fill(0x0102)))
  app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
    console.log(String(err))
    next(err)
  })
  const server = app.listen(0)
  await new Promise((resolve) => server.once('listening', resolve))
  const res = await fetch(`http://localhost:${server.address().port}`)
  const body = Buffer.from(await res.arrayBuffer())
  const shown = res.status === 200 ? `${body.length} bytes: ${body.toString('hex').slice(0, 16)}` : ''
  console.log(`etag ${etag}, ${length} elements -> ${res.status} ${shown}`.trimEnd())
  server.close()
}

;(async () => {
  await run(true, 2)
  await run(false, 2)
  await run(false, 1000)
})()
```

Output with `NODE_ENV=test`, which stops Express from logging the error a second time:

```
etag true, 2 elements -> 200 2 bytes: 0202
TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]: The "chunk" argument must be of type string or an instance of Buffer or Uint8Array. Received an instance of Uint16Array
etag false, 2 elements -> 500
etag false, 1000 elements -> 200 1000 bytes: 0202020202020202
```

The second line is the error that the error handler logs.

## What is the expected behavior?

The same behavior with ETag on or off, and for any length. The response is either all the bytes of the array or a clear error.

## What do you see instead?

- With ETag (the default): status 200, but each element is cut to its low byte. Half of the data is lost.
- Without ETag and fewer than 1000 elements: status 500.
- Without ETag and 1000 elements or more: status 200, with the same lost data as with ETag.

## Additional information

`res.send()` accepts any `ArrayBuffer.isView()` value as binary data ([`lib/response.js:151`](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/0dee2c52c7c873498f8ed7d8ee4ddd0a04d3ada8/lib/response.js#L151)). Then the value goes one of two ways ([line 170](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/0dee2c52c7c873498f8ed7d8ee4ddd0a04d3ada8/lib/response.js#L170)):

- `Buffer.from(chunk, encoding)` ([line 175](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/0dee2c52c7c873498f8ed7d8ee4ddd0a04d3ada8/lib/response.js#L175)), when ETag is on or the array has 1000 elements or more. For a typed array, `Buffer.from()` copies the element values, not the bytes.
- Directly to `this.end()` ([line 218](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/0dee2c52c7c873498f8ed7d8ee4ddd0a04d3ada8/lib/response.js#L218)), when ETag is off and the array is small. Node only accepts a string, a `Buffer` or a `Uint8Array` there, so it throws.

Support for `Uint8Array` came in 5.1.0 (#6285). Express 4.22.3 sends a typed array as JSON, so this affects 5.1.0 and later.

This came up in other PRs:

- #7433, closed without a merge, was changed to keep the truncated output for compatibility.
- In #7511, @peralva noted the truncation and proposed `Buffer.from(chunk.buffer, chunk.byteOffset, chunk.byteLength)` for every view. The author kept multi-byte typed arrays out of that PR, as a follow-up for the maintainers to decide.
- A review on #7410 noted that its change would make the 500 the default.

This issue is for that follow-up. Sending the bytes of the view, as @peralva proposed, or limiting binary support to `Uint8Array`, changes the response for these arrays. So I did not open a PR. Happy to open one in the direction you prefer 🙌
items.title: res.send() with a non-Uint8Array typed array loses data, or returns 500 without ETag

Hi! 🙂 `req.subdomains` splits an IPv6 host that contains dots.

## Environment information

**Version**: express 5.3.0 (4.22.3 gives the same result)

**Platform**: Darwin 27.0.0

**Node.js version**: v24.21.0

**Any other relevant information**: None.

## What steps will reproduce the bug?

`req.subdomains` does not split a host that is an IP address. This works for `[::1]`. An IPv6 address can also contain dots, for example the IPv4-mapped address `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`. `req.subdomains` splits that host on the dots:

```js
const express = require('express')
const app = express()

app.get('/', (req, res) => res.json(req.subdomains))
app.listen(3000)
```

```bash
curl -H 'Host: [::1]' http://localhost:3000/
# []

curl -H 'Host: [::ffff:127.0.0.1]' http://localhost:3000/
# ["0","[::ffff:127"]
```

Full repro, with `npm run repro`: https://github.com/johnnyhuirilef/expressjs-repros/tree/main/subdomains-ipv6-dotted-host

Note: `fetch()` rewrites the host to `[::ffff:7f00:1]`, so it does not show the bug. curl, `http.get()` and `X-Forwarded-Host` (with `trust proxy`) send the host as written.

## What is the expected behavior?

`[]` for `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`, the same as for `[::1]`. With `subdomain offset` set to `0`, the expected value is `["[::ffff:127.0.0.1]"]`.

## What do you see instead?

`["0","[::ffff:127"]`. With `subdomain offset` set to `0`: `["1]","0","0","[::ffff:127"]`.

## Additional information

`req.hostname` keeps the brackets of an IPv6 literal. `req.subdomains` passes that value to `net.isIP()` in `lib/request.js`, and `isIP('[::ffff:127.0.0.1]')` returns `0`. The existing `[::1]` test passes only because that address has no dots.

I have a fix with tests. Happy to open a PR 🙌

`res.send()` stopped adding `Content-Length` when a `Transfer-Encoding` header is present (#4893, #7459), because the two must not be sent together (RFC 9112 §6.2). `res.redirect()` still sets `Content-Length` unconditionally, so it produces the same invalid response:

```js
app.use((req, res) => {
  res.set('Transfer-Encoding', 'chunked')
  res.redirect('http://google.com')
})
```

Node's HTTP client rejects the response with `Parse Error: Content-Length can't be present with Transfer-Encoding`.

Expected: `res.redirect()` follows the same rule as `res.send()` and omits `Content-Length` when `Transfer-Encoding` is set.
items.title: res.redirect() sets Content-Length when Transfer-Encoding is already set

The existing res.status implementation correctly accepts the inclusive 100-999 range and rejects out-of-range integers. The regression tests can observe Node's later HTTP validation instead of Express's own synchronous validation.

At 7ef98448f8b38099ab1ded55e458538ad47a51e7, temporarily replacing the range condition in lib/response.js with if (false) leaves the existing HTTP checks for 99 and 1000 passing: Node rejects those values when the response ends, with an error matching the existing expectation.

The test-only correction is to assert directly that Object.create(express.response).status(99) and status(1000) raise RangeError, while keeping the HTTP checks. Direct tests also cover acceptance of 100 and 999, the returned response object, and the stored statusCode. Testing 100 directly avoids interim-response behavior over HTTP.

Reproduction:

1. Run npm run lint and npm run test-ci on the proposed tests: 1,263 tests pass.
2. In an isolated copy, temporarily replace code < 100 || code > 999 in res.status with false.
3. The two direct rejection assertions fail with Missing expected exception (RangeError). Without those direct assertions, the HTTP tests stay green.
4. Restore the condition; all tests pass.

Prepared with AI assistance using [Supertest](https://github.com/renanmpimentel/supertest), a test-effectiveness audit skill. Its concrete benefit here was revealing a validation regression hidden by the HTTP boundary and verifying that the strengthened tests detect it. This report concerns test coverage; application behavior is unchanged.

Environment: Express 5.2.1, Node 24.13.0, Linux.
items.title: Regression tests can miss res.status range-validation failures

## Description

With Node.js 22+ supporting native TypeScript via `--experimental-strip-types`, it would be beneficial if Express could support TypeScript source files directly.

## Proposed Solution

1. Detect `.ts` files in routes directory automatically
2. Use Node.js native TypeScript stripping when available
3. Fall back to tsx/ts-node when native support is unavailable
4. Provide TypeScript-first API definitions

## Benefits

- Zero-config TypeScript setup
- Faster development iteration
- Better DX for TypeScript users
- Reduced build tooling complexity

## Additional Context

This would align Express with modern development practices and attract more TypeScript developers.

## Description

Express depends on `body-parser@^2.2.1`, which resolves to a version affected by
**CVE-2026-12590** (GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6). body-parser `>=2.0.0 <2.3.0` fails open
when given an invalid `limit` option value — `bytes.parse()` returns `null` and
request body size enforcement is silently disabled, allowing a DoS via oversized
payloads. This is flagged by scanners such as Trivy.

## Expected

`body-parser` resolves to the patched `2.3.0`, which throws on an invalid `limit`
at parser initialization.

## Fix

A fix is proposed in #7390, which bumps the dependency to `body-parser@^2.3.0`.

## References
- https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-12590
- https://github.com/expressjs/body-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6
items.title: body-parser < 2.3.0 fails open on invalid `limit` (CVE-2026-12590)

## Environment information

**Version**: `5.2.1` (also present on the `4.x` line — same `req.fresh` implementation)

**Platform**: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

**Node.js version**: `v24.18.0` (QUERY requires Node >= 22, where `http.METHODS` includes `QUERY`)

**Any other relevant information**:
`req.fresh` (`lib/request.js`) short-circuits to `false` for any method other than `GET`/`HEAD`, so `res.send`/`res.json` never emit a `304 Not Modified` for a `QUERY` request even when the client sends a matching `If-None-Match`.

As far as I can tell, QUERY is a safe, idempotent, cacheable method whose responses explicitly support conditional revalidation, as per https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc10008/, so it should behave like `GET`/`HEAD` here.

## What steps will reproduce the bug?

Minimal app:

```js
const express = require('express')
const app = express()

app.query('/search', (req, res) => {
  res.set('ETag', '"abc"')
  res.json({ results: [] })
})

app.listen(3000)
```

Send a conditional QUERY with a matching `If-None-Match`:

```sh
# Sends a body (the point of QUERY) and the ETag the server previously returned
curl -i -X QUERY http://localhost:3000/search \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'If-None-Match: "abc"' \
  --data '{"q":"x"}'
```

**Observed:** `200 OK` with the full response body every time.

**Expected:** `304 Not Modified` with an empty body — the same behavior an identical `GET` produces, since the response `ETag` matches the request's `If-None-Match`.

Equivalent reproduction against `req.fresh` directly (mirrors the test suite style):

```js
const app = express()
app.use((req, res) => {
  res.set('ETag', '"12345"')
  res.send(req.fresh) // GET -> true (304); QUERY -> false (200) before the fix
})
// request(app).query('/').set('If-None-Match', '"12345"') => 200 'false', expected 304
```
items.title: req.fresh returns false for QUERY requests, so 304 Not Modified is never sent

items.body:
## Bug

`res.send()` handles `Buffer` and TypedArray (`ArrayBuffer.isView`) as binary data, but a raw `ArrayBuffer` — the standard JavaScript binary data type — falls through to `this.json(chunk)`, producing {}` with `Content-Type: application/json`.

```js
res.send(new ArrayBuffer(10))
// Sends: {} (Content-Type: application/json)
// Expected: 10 zero bytes (Content-Type: application/octet-stream)
```

## Cause

PR #6285 (merged as 55869f49) fixed `Uint8Array`/`DataView` support by adding an `ArrayBuffer.isView()` check. However, `ArrayBuffer.isView(new ArrayBuffer(...))` returns `false`, so raw `ArrayBuffer` was missed.

## Proposed fix

Add an `instanceof ArrayBuffer` check in `lib/response.js` that converts to `Buffer` and sets the binary content type, consistent with the existing `ArrayBuffer.isView` branch.

## Real-world impact

`ArrayBuffer` is the standard binary type used by fetch, Web Crypto, WebSocket, FileReader, and similar APIs. Passing it directly to `res.send()` is a common scenario that currently fails silently.
items.title: res.send(ArrayBuffer) silently sends {} as JSON
